subject: Banking
title: How Interest Rates Move Profits
description: A short lesson to help you apply How Interest Rates Move Profits.

hook.text: When the Fed raises rates, bank profits usually jump. They raise loan rates faster than they raise deposit rates.

buildup.text: A 1% rate hike might add 1% to mortgage rates immediately. But your savings account rate climbs by just 0.25%.

discovery.text: This lag is called deposit beta. Banks deliberately delay passing rate increases to savers to widen their spread.

twist.text: When rates fall, the opposite happens. Banks drop loan rates slowly and slash deposit rates immediately.

climax.text: Banks always adjust rates in their favor. Rising or falling, the timing benefits the bank, not the depositor.

punchline.text: Rates up: your savings lag. Rates down: your savings fall first.

quiz.question: What is 'deposit beta'?
options: The delay in passing rate increases to depositors

details.summary: Bank profits are heavily influenced by interest rate levels and the yield curve shape. Rising rates generally boost bank earnings by widening the gap between what they pay depositors and charge borrowers, until rates rise high enough to trigger loan defaults.
details.whyItMatters: Interest rates are the single most important driver of bank profitability. Understanding this relationship explains why bank stocks rise on rate hikes and why inverted yield curves signal trouble for the banking sector.
takeaways: Banks profit from the spread between deposit rates paid and loan rates earned
A steeper yield curve means higher margins for banks
Rising rates boost income initially but eventually increase loan default risk

faq.question: Why do rising interest rates help bank profits?
faq.answer: Banks can raise loan rates immediately but are slow to increase deposit rates. This expands the spread between what they earn on loans and pay on deposits. Higher rates also increase returns on the bank's investment portfolio.

faq.question: When do rising rates hurt banks?
faq.answer: If rates rise too fast, borrowers default on adjustable-rate loans, bond portfolios lose value, and depositors demand higher rates or flee. The 2023 bank failures showed how rapidly rising rates can destroy banks holding long-term low-rate bonds.
